question: What does the term "checkmate" refer to in chess?
solution:
The correct answer is __**End of game**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In chess, "checkmate" occurs when the king is in a position to be captured (in check) and there is no legal move to remove the threat of capture.
 
• The term signifies the end of the game, with the player delivering the checkmate declared the winner.
 
• A checkmate can occur at any stage of the game—opening, middle-game, or endgame—depending on the players' strategies.
 
• The word "checkmate" originates from the Persian phrase "Shah Mat," meaning "the king is dead" or "the king is helpless."
 
• It is one of the primary objectives of chess, emphasizing strategic planning and tactical execution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Check**: A situation in chess where the king is under direct threat of capture, but the threat can still be countered.
 
• **Stalemate**: A situation where a player has no legal moves left, but their king is not in check, resulting in a draw.
 
• **Resignation**: A player may resign the game voluntarily if they believe they cannot avoid checkmate or turn the game in their favor.
 
• **Chess Notation**: Moves leading to checkmate are often denoted with the "#" symbol in algebraic notation. For example, "Qh5#."
 
• **Famous Checkmates**: Many classic games and puzzles focus on delivering checkmate in a specific number of moves, known as "mate-in-x" problems.
